candidates.source_name: The Middle East and Global Energy Markets – Topics - IEA
candidates.snippet:
Current market backdrop
Physical crude markets have continued to reflect acute supply tightness as refiners scramble to replace lost Middle Eastern cargoes with alternative supplies. Prices for certain oil products – notably diesel, jet fuel and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), which have been particularly exposed to the disruption – have remained elevated.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have successfully redirected some exports to terminals loading outside of the Strait of Hormuz. Producers outside the Middle East have also pushed output higher and lifted exports to record levels in response to the crisis.
Gulf producers exported 3.3 million barrels per day of refined oil products and 1.5 million barrels per day of LPG in 2025. Nearly 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity in the region has been shut due to attacks and a lack of viable export outlets.
On 11 March, IEA Member countries unanimously agreed to take emergency collective action to respond to the major disruptions in oil markets, making 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available – the largest-ever release coordinated by the Agency.
Why is the Strait of Hormuz so important?
Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have operational crude pipelines that could potentially reroute flows to bypass the Strait, with an estimated 3.5 million barrels per day to 5.5 million barrels per day of available capacity.

candidates.title: U.S. Army Has Failed To Replenish Stockpiles Of 155mm Artillery Rounds
candidates.source_name: U.S. Army Has Failed To Replenish Stockpiles Of 155mm Artillery Rounds
candidates.snippet:
The U.S. military faces critical ordnance shortages, with precision munitions like Tomahawks and Patriots significantly depleted, and over three million 155mm artillery rounds sent to Ukraine. Despite a Biden administration goal to boost 155mm production to 100,000 rounds monthly by October 2025, current output is only 36,000.
The United States military has burned through vast stockpiles of its ordnance, notably of its precision munitions and interceptors, specifically Tomahawk cruise missiles, Patriot air defense systems and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors.
The ongoing conflict with Iran has seen more than 1,000 Tomahawks fired, exhausting roughly 10 times the annual procurement rate.
Inventories of the Patriot and THADD have been depleted by nearly 50%.
Since February 2022, when Russia launched its unprovoked invasion, the U.S. military saw its stockpile significantly depleted. More than three million were sent to aid Kyiv’s war effort alone.
A newly released report from the Pentagon’s Office of the Inspector General found that the General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems facility in Mesquite, Texas, one of the facilities built specifically to produce 155mm artillery rounds, has not delivered the necessary components.
That plant, which opened to significant fanfare in May 2024, cost U.S. taxpayers around $469 million and has failed to produce any of the metal projectile parts required in the production of the 155mm artillery round.

Ukraine’s military intelligence has estimated that Russia produced about 2 million 122mm and 152mm artillery rounds last year, while importing an additional 2.7 million from North Korea.

RTX describes it as a low-cost, rail-launched missile variant using a boost rocket motor and a turbine engine for high-speed counter-UAS missions, while the Army identifies it as a ground-launched, radar-guided interceptor available in kinetic and non-kinetic forms.
Bloomberg reports that a Patriot interceptor used against ballistic missiles costs about $4 million per shot, while a Coyote shot is about $120,000. That does not make Coyote “cheap” in a commercial sense, but in military magazine-depth terms it is a far more sustainable answer to the routine drone raid.
What makes the new deal strategically important is that it connects tactical necessity to industrial policy. The Army already awarded RTX $75 million in January 2024 for 600 Coyote 2C interceptors under rapid acquisition authority, explicitly to meet growing counter-UAS demand.

Leveraged loan issuers increase amend-and-extend deals to take out credit facilities
Richard Kellerhals
June 17, 2026 3 min read
Amend-and-extend loan volume jumped to $25.4 billion in May, a high for any month since June 2024, according to LCD.
May's amend-and-extend activity came via 19 transactions, up from 18 transactions (for $13.6 billion) in April.
Nearly $79 billion of volume this year is up from roughly $68 billion through the first five months of 2025.
Borrowers continued to seek amendments, as opposed to refinancings, to take out credit facilities.
The average yield to maturity for refinancing institutional term loans via syndication currently stands at 6.7% for 2026, which is lower than 7.4% in 2025 and the 8.6% in 2024, but still elevated from all the years spanning 2011-2022.
While there is heightened urgency to address near-term maturities, LCD data show that the companies being given breathing room are, by and large, not immediate default candidates. Roughly 71% of the amendments completed in 2026 were rated B-minus or higher at the issuer level. However, that's down from the 77% in 2025 and 84% in 2024.
In 2025, sponsored and non-sponsored companies with pro rata loans were focused on extending 2026 and 2027 maturities — extending $37.6 billion of debt due in 2027 and $36.7 billion due in 2026, along with $13.8 billion due in 2028.

candidates.title: Scaling the repayment wall in private credit - Crisil Integral IQ
candidates.source_name: Scaling the repayment wall in private credit - Crisil Integral IQ
candidates.snippet:
* The private market is staring at a wall of repayments while contracting even more debt: Morgan Stanley estimates maturities in the United States (US) middle market direct lending and business development companies (BDCs) at roughly $475 billion till 2033, with 2028-2031 seeing the maximum concentration and roughly $260 billion maturing in
2026-2029
February 2026. Moody's also revised its outlook on US BDCs to negative on April 7, 2026, citing redemption pressure, higher leverage and weaker funding access.
The maturity wall should surface first as a refinancing and structuring challenge, not as a broad market shutdown.
The reason is straightforward: Most loans have floating rates and are backed by sponsors, ensuring the outcomes are driven to a lesser degree by aggregate debt volumes than by a combination of cash-interest burden, operating momentum, sector-specific disruption and lender willingness to extend or re-paper the capital structure.
Overall, lending stress will be sector-driven largely.
Amend-and-extend transactions, PIK toggles, incremental liquidity, covenant resets, layering of capital and sponsor-supported bridges are likely to matter more than plain-vanilla new-money growth issuance. Vehicle-level liquidity management is also becoming a more important differentiator.
For a private credit investor, this means there is an opportunity to widen the spread through refinancing, amendment and restructuring capabilities rather than pure growth underwriting.

Private Credit BDCs’ 2028 Maturity Wall Poses Risk, Moody’s Says
Private credit funds with outsized exposure to software and tech loans face rising refinancing and credit risks as a wave of debt maturities loom from 2028, according to Moody’s Ratings.
Business development companies, which lend directly to middle-market businesses, may see “a particular challenge” for leveraged software borrowers amid fresh concerns about inflation and the threat of AI disruption, according to a report released Wednesday by the credit-rating company.

Global Refinancing: Brisk Issuance Pushes Speculative-Grade Maturity Peak Out To 2031
The peak maturity year for speculative-grade nonfinancial corporate debt has been pushed out to 2031 globally, in a rapid shift from 2029 in April and 2028 in January of this year.
A surge of new bond issuance in the first half of 2026, led by fundraising activity to support the buildout of AI and digital infrastructure, boosted global nonfinancial maturities in 2031, while steady refinancing activity reduced speculative-grade maturities through 2029.
While we view near-term maturities as increasingly manageable, potential challenges remain on the horizon--maturities of debt rated 'B-' and lower rise to $268.8 billion in 2028, much of which is concentrated in the U.S. and in the healthcare, high technology, and media and entertainment sectors.
